blocks.text: ⁧البَيْتُ الكَبِيرُ⁩ means "the big house"; ⁧البَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ⁩ means "the house" is large. The difference lies in an article. In this unit you learn to distinguish the syntagma (name + adjective, a piece of phrase) from the nominal sentence (subject + predicate), to say It is the distinction that will allow you to read any newspaper title correctly. Two weeks.

chapters.title: 3. The syntagma: the adjective also copies the determination

blocks.text: The attribute adjective agrees with the name in general (A1-03) and in determination: if the name has the article, the adjective also takes it.

rows: a big house · the big house
a new car · the new car

blocks.text: Because that's how it works. For Arabic the adjective is a name that repeats what precedes it: it follows it as an echo, with the same genre, the same determination and the same case. If the echo doesn't have the article while the name does, the link breaks and becomes another structure: the phrase.

chapters.title: 4. Syntagma or phrase: the four combinations

blocks.text: The golden rule of the nominal phrase. The subject is usually determined and the predicate undetermined. The point at which the determination is interrupted is the boundary between subject and predicate: in ⁧البَيْتُ الكَبِيرُ جَمِيلٌ⁩ the article reaches up to ⁧الكَبِيرُ⁩ , so the predicate is ⁧جَمِيلٌ⁩ . How to read it in a text without vowels. ⁧البيت الكبير⁩ = syntagma; ⁧البيت كبير⁩ = sentence. The article is also seen without vowels: it's your first analysis tool. To be recognized. When even the predicate is determined, a pronoun often fits between the two parts to mark the border: ⁧البَيْتُ هُوَ الكَبِيرُ⁩ The house is the big one. You'll meet him in the press.
An indefinite name does not normally open a nominal phrase. To say "there is a car in the street" it first puts the place:

rows: There's a car in the street.
There is an ancient university in the city.
There's a mosque in the street.

blocks.text: Two streets. ⁧فِي⁩ + place + indeterminate name is the basic construction. ⁧هُنَاكَ⁩ , that in A1-02 It means "there" here it works as "there": it is very used in the media language. With a determined subject you return to the normal order: ⁧السَّيَّارَةُ فِي الشَّارِعِ⁩ The car is on the road.
